source_text: εὖ μάλα καὶ τὰ δι' ὧν ἂν γένοιτο ταυτὶ, πορισμοὶ χρημάτων, τῇ τῆς ἐνδείας ἐφόδῳ μαχόμενοι, εὐναί τε μαλακαὶ, καὶ τὰ τούτοις ἀγχοῦ. Ἀλλ' εἰ καὶ χρειώδη ταῦτα καὶ ἀναγκαῖα τοῖς ἐπὶ γῆς καὶ ἐν σώμασιν, ἀλλ' οὖν τοῖς ἁγίοις λελόγισται παρ' οὐδὲν, ὄχλον δὲ ὥσπερ εἰκαῖον ἁπλῶς τὴν τῶν τοιούτων κτῆσιν ἀποπεμψάμενοι, μονονουχὶ γυμνοῖς καὶ ἀναμφιάστοις σώμασι διατελοῦσιν ἐν κόσμῳ, τὸ προστυχὸν καὶ εὐπόριστον τῇ τῆς σαρκὸς ἀνάγκῃ σὺν ὄκνῳ δωρούμενοι. Ἀποτετιλμένων δὲ τῶν πτερῶν, καὶ ἐξῃρημένης τῆς φύσης, ἤτοι τοῦ προλόβου, καὶ ἐκκλάσει, φησὶν, ἀπὸ τῶν πτερυγίων, καὶ οὐ διελεῖ, καὶ ἀνοίσει λοιπὸν ἐπὶ τὸ θυσιαστήριον. Καὶ ἡ μὲν τῶν πτερυγίων ἔκκλασις, τύπος ἂν εἴη καὶ ὑπόδειγμα σαφὲς τοῦ μὴ φρονεῖν τὰ ὑπέρογκα, μήτε μὴν ὑψοῦ πέτασθαι τῶν ἁγίων τὸν νοῦν, συνεπάγεσθαι δὲ μᾶλλον τοῖς ταπεινοῖς, καὶ οἱονεὶ τὰ κάτω ζητεῖν. Μετέωρος γὰρ ἀείπως ἐστὶ τῶν ἀλαζόνων ὁ νοῦς, καὶ πρὸς τὰ ἄνω φέρεται, συνιζῆσαι τοῖς χθαμαλωτέροις οὐκ ἀνεχόμενος, καὶ τὸ μέτριόν τε καὶ ταπεινὸν ἀτιμάζων φρόνημα. Οὐκοῦν ἡ τῶν πτερυγίων ἔκκλασις, ἀλαζονείας ἀπόθεσιν αἰνιγματωδῶς ὑποφαίνει· ὅτι δὲ καὶ εἰσάπαν, καὶ, ἵν' οὕτως εἴπωμεν, ὁλοτρόπως ἀνέθεσαν τῷ Θεῷ τὴν οἰκείαν ζωὴν, οὐ μεμερισμένοι πρὸς τὰ ἐν κόσμῳ, τὸ μὴ διαιρεῖσθαι δηλοῖ· μεμερίσθαι δὲ τοὺς ἐν γάμῳ, καὶ ὁ σοφὸς ἔφη Παῦλος. Ἱερὸς οὖν ἄρα τῶν ἁγίων ὁ νοῦς, ζωή τε ἁγία, καὶ τρυφῆς ἀμείνων σωματικῆς, καὶ μερίμνης κοσμικῆς ἐλευθέρα, καὶ φρονήματι τῷ μετρίῳ περικαλλής· ἀμέριστος δὲ καὶ πρὸς τὰ ἐν κόσμῳ. Τοιγάρτοι καὶ εἰς ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας ἀνατίθεται τῷ Θεῷ. {ΠΑΛΛ.} Ὧδε ἔχει. {ΚΥΡ.} Καταβιβάζει δὲ τῆς θυσίας τοὺς τρόπους, καὶ πρὸς τὰ ἔτι μείω τε καὶ παντὶ τῷ ἔτει λοιπὸν ἐγκείμενα, καὶ οὐ σὺν ἱδρῶτι ληπτὰ κατευρύνων, οἶμαί που, μικρῷ καὶ μεγάλῳ τῆς εὐδοκιμήσεως τὴν ὁδόν· γέγραπται γὰρ, ὅτι «Πλατεῖα ἡ ἐντολή σου σφόδρα.» Καὶ οὐ τῷ μεγέθει τῆς καρποφορίας πάντη τε καὶ πάντως τὸ γνήσιον κρίνεται, παρά γε τῷ φιλαρέτῳ Θεῷ, ἀλλ' ἐν ἴσῳ τοῖς προὔχουσιν ὁ βραχὺς, τὰ ἐνόντα διδοὺς, καὶ οἷς ἂν ἔχοι καὶ δύναιτο τιμᾷν ᾑρημένος. Ἔφη τοίνυν ὧδε πάλιν· «Ἐὰν δὲ ψυχὴ προσφέρῃ δῶ-ρον θυσίαν τῷ Κυρίῳ, σεμίδαλις ἔσται τὸ δῶρον αὐτοῦ· καὶ ἐπιχεεῖ ἐπ' αὐτὸ ἔλαιον, καὶ ἐπιθήσει ἐπ' αὐτὸ λίβανον, θυσία ἐστί· καὶ οἴσει πρὸς τοὺς υἱοὺς Ἀαρὼν τοὺς ἱερεῖς, καὶ δραξάμενος ἀπ' αὐτῆς πλήρη τὴν δράκα ἀπὸ τῆς σεμιδάλεως σὺν τῷ ἐλαίῳ, καὶ πᾶν τὸ λίβανον αὐτῆς, καὶ ἐπιθήσει ὁ ἱερεὺς τὸ μνημόσυνον αὐτῆς ἐπὶ τὸ θυσιαστήριον, θυσία ἐστὶν, ὀσμὴ εὐωδίας τῷ Κυρίῳ.» Συνίης οὖν ὅπως τὸ τοῦ προσκομίζοντος ὑπέμνησε ταπεινόν· ψυχὴν γὰρ ἁπλῶς, κἂν εἰ πολὺ τὸ ἄσημον ἔχοι κατὰ τόνδε τὸν βίον, ὁ θεῖος ἡμῖν ὀνομάζει νόμος, τὸ τῆς ἀνωτάτω φύσεως περὶ πάντας ἶσον καὶ ἀπροκλινὲς κἀν τούτῳ δεικνὺς, καθάπερ ἀμέλει καὶ ἐν τῷ φάναι πάλιν, ὅτι «Πᾶσαι αἱ ψυχαὶ, ἐμαί εἰσιν.» Ἀπροσωπόληπτον γὰρ τὸ θεῖον, καθάπερ ἔφην ἀρτίως. Οὐκοῦν εἴπερ ἕλοιτό τις τῶν οὐκ ἐχόντων, φησὶ, τὸ ἐπιφανὲς ἐν κόσμῳ, δωροφορεῖν τῷ Θεῷ, σεμίδαλις ἔσται τῆς θυσίας ὁ τρόπος. πλὴν ἐλαιόδευτος καὶ ἀναμὶξ λιβάνῳ· ὅτι
pass_a_gloss: [continuing the list] very well also the things through which these would come about: acquisitions of money (πορισμοὶ χρημάτων), fighting the onset (ἔφοδος) of want (ἔνδεια), and soft beds (εὐναὶ μαλακαί), and the things near these. But if these are useful (χρειώδης) and necessary for those on earth and in bodies, yet for the saints they have been reckoned (λογίζομαι, pf.) as nothing; having sent away (ἀποπέμπω) the possession (κτῆσις) of such things as a pointless crowd/nuisance (ὄχλος εἰκαῖος), they continue in the world with bodies all but (μονονουχί) naked and unclothed (ἀναμφίαστος), giving to the necessity (ἀνάγκη) of the flesh what is at hand (προστυχές) and easily got (εὐπόριστον), with reluctance (ὄκνος). The feathers having been plucked (ἀποτίλλω), and the craw (φύσα), that is the crop (πρόλοβος), removed, and he will break it, he says, from the wings (πτερύγια), and will not divide, and will then carry it up (ἀναφέρω) to the altar [Lev 1:17]. The breaking (ἔκκλασις) of the wings would be a type and clear example (ὑπόδειγμα) of not thinking (φρονέω) overweening things (ὑπέρογκα), nor the mind of the saints flying (πέτομαι) on high, but rather being led along with (συνεπάγομαι) the lowly (ταπεινοί), and as it were seeking the things below [Rom 12:16]. For the mind of the boasters (ἀλαζόνες) is always somehow lofty (μετέωρος) and borne to things above, not enduring to sit down with (συνιζάνω) the lower (χθαμαλώτεροι), and dishonoring the measured and humble mind-set (φρόνημα). So the breaking of the wings shows in riddle (αἰνιγματωδῶς) the putting off (ἀπόθεσις) of boastfulness (ἀλαζονεία). And that wholly, and so to speak in every manner (ὁλοτρόπως), they dedicated (ἀνατίθημι) to God their own life, not divided (μερίζω) toward the things in the world, the not being divided (διαιρέω) shows; that those in marriage (γάμος) are divided, the wise Paul also said [1 Cor 7:33-34]. Sacred then the mind of the saints, and holy life, better than bodily luxury, free of worldly care (μέριμνα), very beautiful (περικαλλής) with measured mind-set; undivided (ἀμέριστος) toward things in the world. Therefore it is dedicated to God for a smell of fragrance. PALL.: So it is. CYR.: He brings down (καταβιβάζω) the modes (τρόποι) of sacrifice even to things smaller and lying at hand (ἐγκείμαι) all year, and taken without sweat (ἱδρώς), widening (κατευρύνω), I think, for small and great the road of good repute/approval (εὐδοκίμησις); for it is written: Broad (πλατεῖα) your commandment (ἐντολή) exceedingly [Ps 118:96 LXX]. And not by the size of the fruit-bearing (καρποφορία) in every way and altogether is genuineness (τὸ γνήσιον) judged with the virtue-loving (φιλάρετος) God, but the small (βραχύς) [is] equal to the eminent (προέχοντες), giving what he has, and having chosen to honor (τιμάω) with what he has and is able. He said again thus: If a soul (ψυχή) brings a gift, a sacrifice to the Lord, fine flour (σεμίδαλις) will be his gift; and he will pour oil (ἔλαιον) on it, and put frankincense (λίβανος) on it; it is a sacrifice; and he will bring it to the sons of Aaron the priests, and grasping (δράσσομαι) from it the full handful (δράξ) of the fine flour with the oil, and all its frankincense, the priest will put its memorial (μνημόσυνον) on the altar; it is a sacrifice, a smell of fragrance to the Lord [Lev 2:1-2 LXX]. Do you understand how it reminded of (ὑπομιμνῄσκω) the lowliness (τὸ ταπεινόν) of the bringer (προσκομίζων)? For simply a soul, even if he should have much obscurity (τὸ ἄσημον) in this life, the divine law names, showing also in this the equal (ἴσον) and unbiased (ἀπροκλινές) [disposition] of the highest nature (ἀνωτάτω φύσις) toward all, as indeed also in saying again: All the souls are mine [Ezek 18:4]. For impartial (ἀπροσωπόληπτον) the divine (τὸ θεῖον), as I said just now. So if one of those not having the conspicuous (ἐπιφανές) in the world, he says, chooses to bring gifts (δωροφορέω) to God, fine flour will be the mode of sacrifice, but oil-moistened (ἐλαιόδευτος) and mixed with frankincense; that [ὅτι: continues in section 8].
pass_b_english: Cyril: …certainly also the means by which these are obtained, ways of earning money that fight off the onset of want; and soft beds, and whatever is close to these. But even if these things are useful and necessary for those who live on earth and in bodies, the saints count them as nothing. They have sent away the possession of such things as so much useless clutter, and they pass their lives in the world with bodies all but naked and unclothed, granting grudgingly to the needs of the flesh whatever comes to hand and is easily obtained. When the feathers have been plucked and the craw, that is, the crop, has been removed, ‘he shall break it,’ it says, ‘at the wings, and shall not divide it’ (Leviticus 1:17), and then he shall carry it up onto the altar. The breaking of the wings would be a type and a clear example of the mind of the saints not thinking proud thoughts, nor flying on high, but rather being drawn along with the lowly (Romans 12:16) and seeking, so to speak, the things below. For the mind of the arrogant is always lifted up somehow and carried toward the heights; it cannot bear to sit down with those of lower station, and it despises a modest and humble way of thinking. So the breaking of the wings shows in a figure the putting away of arrogance. And that it is not divided shows that they have dedicated their own life to God entirely and, if we may put it so, in every way, not divided toward the things of the world; and the wise Paul too said that those who are married are divided (1 Corinthians 7:33–34). Holy, then, is the mind of the saints, and holy their life: above bodily indulgence, free of worldly care, made beautiful by a modest mind, and undivided toward the things of the world. That is why it is dedicated to God as a fragrant aroma.

Cyril: He then brings the kinds of sacrifice down further, to things smaller still, things that are at hand all year round and are got without sweat, widening, I think, the road to approval for small and great alike. For it is written: ‘Your commandment is exceedingly broad’ (Psalm 119:96). With God, who loves virtue, sincerity is not judged in every case and altogether by the size of the offering; rather, the lowly person stands equal with the eminent when he gives what he has and has chosen to honor God with whatever he has and is able to give. So he spoke again in this way: ‘If a soul brings a gift, a sacrifice to the Lord, his gift shall be fine flour; and he shall pour oil on it and put frankincense on it; it is a sacrifice. And he shall bring it to the sons of Aaron, the priests; and taking from it a full handful of the fine flour with the oil, and all its frankincense, the priest shall put its memorial portion on the altar; it is a sacrifice, a fragrant aroma to the Lord’ (Leviticus 2:1–2). Do you see, then, how it pointed to the lowliness of the one who brings the offering? For the divine law simply names him ‘a soul’, even if he is quite undistinguished in this life, and in this too it shows that the supreme nature is fair and impartial toward all, as indeed it does again when it says: ‘All souls are mine’ (Ezekiel 18:4). For the Godhead shows no partiality, as I said just now. So if one of those who have no distinction in the world, it says, chooses to bring a gift to God, fine flour will be the form of the sacrifice, but moistened with oil and mixed with frankincense.

anf_compare.notes: No public-domain English of De adoratione Book 16. Translated afresh from the PG 68 Greek on 2026-10-23; the withdrawn English was not used for wording.

apparatus.note: PG OCR; a column may cut mid-sentence or mid-word.

Boundary in: section 7 opens inside the list begun in section 6 (‘I mean clothing, and what serves for food, and besides these…’); its first words εὖ μάλα καὶ τὰ δι’ ὧν ἂν γένοιτο ταυτί are rendered ‘certainly also the means by which these are obtained’ (the ‘and’ is already in section 6’s ‘and besides these…’). πορισμοὶ χρημάτων is in apposition to ‘the means’; εὐναί τε μαλακαί resumes the main list, hence the semicolon. Boundary out: the section ends with the single word ὅτι, which begins a sentence finished in section 8 (ὅτι δὲ ζωῆς μὲν εἰς τύπον ἡ σεμίδαλις … πολὺς ἡμῖν διεσάφησε λόγος, ‘That the fine flour is a type of life … we have explained at length’). ‘That’ is rendered at the start of section 8 so the reading text does not end on a dangling word. Leviticus 1:17 quoted in part (ἐκκλάσει … ἀπὸ τῶν πτερυγίων, καὶ οὐ διελεῖ); ‘carry it up onto the altar’ is Cyril’s paraphrase of the same verse. Romans 12:16 (μὴ τὰ ὑψηλὰ φρονοῦντες ἀλλὰ τοῖς ταπεινοῖς συναπαγόμενοι) is a clear verbal allusion (συνεπάγεσθαι τοῖς ταπεινοῖς), so it is cited. ‘Seeks the things below’ reverses the wording of Colossians 3:1–2 in the sense of humility; not cited. 1 Corinthians 7:33–34 (καὶ μεμέρισται): Paul says the married man is divided; Cyril generalizes to ‘those who are married’. Psalm 119:96: LXX Psalm 118:96 πλατεῖα ἡ ἐντολή σου σφόδρα = English Psalm 119:96. Leviticus 2:1–2 follows the LXX; ψυχή (‘a soul’) is kept literally because Cyril’s comment rests on that word. The participle δραξάμενος has no finite verb of its own in the LXX; rendered ‘taking from it … the priest shall put’. Ezekiel 18:4 LXX πᾶσαι αἱ ψυχαὶ ἐμαί εἰσιν. Uncited possible allusions: God shows no partiality (Acts 10:34; Romans 2:11; 1 Peter 1:17 ἀπροσωπολήμπτως); giving according to what one has (2 Corinthians 8:12; the widow’s offering, Mark 12:41–44). τὸ θεῖον rendered ‘the Godhead’ (capitalized, meaning God). ‘As I said just now’ refers to Cyril’s words two sentences earlier in this same turn (τὸ … ἶσον καὶ ἀπροκλινές, ‘fair and impartial toward all’). ὄχλος εἰκαῖος rendered ‘useless clutter’; σὺν ὄκνῳ ‘grudgingly’. ‘Is drawn along’ keeps the passive συνεπάγεσθαι. The source shows δῶ-ρον split by a line break; read as δῶρον. ἐκκλάσει rendered ‘break it’ (not ‘break it open’) to match section 6 and Cyril’s reading of the breaking of the wings. The τοῦ μὴ φρονεῖν … ζητεῖν infinitives are kept as the content of the ‘type and clear example’ (‘of the mind of the saints not thinking …’) rather than turned into a separate indicative statement.
